agree.reason: The sales record, the firm floor and the concrete commitments give a sympathetic editor reason to go above budget. But nothing explains why Elena is worth $3,500 more than the $8,000 newcomer, so a resisting editor could still take the cheaper option.

honest.reason: It rightly drops the false claim that every other publisher pays at least $12,000 and invents nothing. It does state the agent's $11,000–$13,000 opinion as a market fact without saying it comes from the agent.

works_the_facts.reason: It places $11,500 at the low end of the range and below the $12,500 paid last year. It never works out stronger figures it could have used: six books at an unchanged fee, about $2,250 a month for four months' work, or what the reading-list book's reprints have earned.

right_comparison.reason: It sets the flat fee over four years against the outside $12,500 and the market range. It does not describe the editor's real alternative, which is losing a proven illustrator whose books reprint and taking on an untested one.

qualification.reason: The commitments carry checkable dates (sketches within six weeks of signing, final art by September 1) and depend on the fee being met. The consequence of a refusal is only implied by 'can't take on another at $9,000.'

objections.reason: The editor's main objections, the $9,000 budget cap and the cheaper newcomer, are never answered head-on. The sales figures and the free spot drawings only address them indirectly.

fit.reason: It is a concise, well-structured email under 250 words, with a subject line and a clear ask.
